name: Separation of Concerns and Layering
intent: Keep code that changes for different reasons in different places, and choose whether to cut the system into horizontal layers, vertical slices or a mix, so that a change touches few files and none of them carries unrelated behaviour.
scenario: A small shop app has orders, invoices and customers. The first version has screen code, business rules and SQL mixed together. The team moves to three layers (controller, service, repository), then finds that renaming an invoice column still edits all three layers. A new architect proposes seven layers, and adding one field to the order screen now edits seven files. A third camp suggests one vertical slice per feature, and restyling every screen then means editing every slice.
problem: "Separate your concerns" is easy to agree with and hard to apply, because a concern is not a layer. Layers cut across features: one feature is spread over every layer, so a change to a feature crosses all of them, and a boundary only pays off if the layers really hide each other's details. Leaky layers (a controller that knows column names) get the cost of layering with none of the isolation. Layers that only forward calls add files without adding separation. Vertical slices keep one feature together, but a change that cuts across features, such as swapping the database, edits every slice. The useful question is which changes actually happen, and which boundary keeps those changes small.

howItWorks.title: Name the concerns by their reasons to change
howItWorks.text: A concern is something that changes for its own reasons: how a screen looks, a pricing rule, how data is queried, which database engine is used. List the changes you really see in this codebase and group the code by them. The separation is useful if one of those changes mostly edits one place.

howItWorks.title: Choose the axis: layers, slices or both
howItWorks.text: Horizontal layers group code by technical role, so changes that cut across features (restyle every screen, swap the database) stay in one layer. Vertical slices group code by feature, so a change to one feature stays in one slice. Neither is better in general: layers favour cross-cutting changes, slices favour feature work, and many teams use slices at the top with a few shared layers underneath.

howItWorks.title: Make each boundary hide something
howItWorks.text: A layer boundary earns its place when the layer above does not know the details below: the controller asks for an order and never sees a column name, and the service never builds SQL. A boundary that lets those details through is a leak, and then a column rename edits every layer, as if the layers did not exist.

howItWorks.title: Check what each layer adds
howItWorks.text: Every layer costs a file per feature, a call to follow and often a copy of the data shape. A layer that only forwards its input to the next one separates nothing, and it turns a one-field change into an edit of every pass-through. Before adding a layer, name the change it will absorb, and drop it if there is none.

howItWorks.title: Test the dependencies when you cut
howItWorks.text: Tests of a layer usually run the layers below it, so a change in a low layer means re-running the tests above it. Layers also give you the choice to replace the lower layer with a fake. Slices keep tests close to the feature but give the feature's code no internal walls. Count both the files edited and the tests re-run before picking.

pros: A change that matches the chosen axis edits few files and leaves unrelated behaviour alone
Hidden details (column names, the database engine) can change without the code above noticing
Each layer can be tested or replaced on its own, for example with a fake repository
Slices give a feature one owner and a small place to read
cons: Every boundary adds files, calls and often a copy of the data shape
A change on the other axis cuts across many files, in layers or in slices
Leaky or pass-through layers cost the same as real ones and separate nothing
The right cut depends on which changes happen, which is a judgement made with incomplete information
whenToUse: Screen code, business rules and queries are tangled so that one fix breaks another concern
You expect to swap or upgrade something below a boundary, such as a database, a payment provider or a UI toolkit
Several people work on the same code and need areas they can change independently
whenNotToUse: A small app or script where the whole flow fits in a few screens of code
As a template applied to every feature: a layer that has no rule or detail to hide is only a forwarder
Before there is any evidence of which change will happen, as a bet on a future that does not arrive
pitfalls: Leaky layers: the controller knows column names, so renaming one column edits every layer
Pass-through layers that copy a record and forward a call, so adding one field edits seven files
Treating layers as the only form of separation, then paying a cross-feature edit for every feature change
Treating vertical slices as free: a database swap or a restyle then edits every slice, each with its unrelated code beside it
Layering by habit, with one controller, service and repository per entity even when the service has no rule
Counting files and forgetting tests: a low-level change re-runs the tests of every layer above it
Sharing one data model through all the layers, so every layer is coupled to the database shape

quiz.question: An invoice column is renamed, and the change edits the controller, the service and the repository. The app has three layers. What does that most likely mean?
options: Three layers are too few, and a fourth layer would absorb the change.
The layers leak: the controller and service know column names that only the repository should know.
That is how layers work, because every change must cross every layer.
The invoice feature should be merged with the order feature.
quiz.explanation: A layer boundary is meant to hide the details below it. If a column name reaches the controller, the rename has to follow it. Another layer would add files without fixing the leak.

quiz.question: A team has a facade, a manager and a domain model layer between its controller and its service, and each only calls the next one. Adding one field to a record now edits seven files. What is the problem?
options: The layers are pass-through: each copies the data shape and hides no detail, so they add edits without adding separation.
Seven layers is too many, and exactly five would be right.
The record should be stored in a different table.
The controller should call the database directly to skip the extra layers.
quiz.explanation: A layer that forwards calls and copies a record separates nothing, and every field change has to be repeated in it. The fix is to remove the layers that hide no detail, not to remove all layers.

quiz.question: A team picks vertical slices, one module per feature. Which change is the most expensive for that choice?
options: Changing the discount rule of one feature.
Adding a field to one feature's screen.
Restyling every screen, or swapping the database engine for all features.
quiz.explanation: Slices keep one feature together, so a change to one feature is cheap. A change that cuts across features has to be made in every slice, and each slice carries unrelated behaviour next to it. Layers show the opposite trade.
